911.title: Gold on the Harmandir
911.hook: he covers the Harmandir in gilded copper and marble, and it becomes the Golden Temple
911.howItsDone: Sikhs visit the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, walk around the pool, listen to kirtan and serve in the langar; the gilded upper walls date from Maharaja Ranjit Singh's time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, a kingdom named for the Khalsa, with coins in the Gurus' names; your line was the khalsa's rule. Today, gold.

Early morning at Amritsar. Mist on the water, kirtan carrying across the pool, and in the middle of it all a building that catches the first light and throws it back gold. People photograph that glow from every side of the pool. But the building wasn't always gold. This path has watched it rise, be desecrated, be blown up, and be rebuilt by the misls with plain hands and hard work. Today, someone covers it in light.
screen: `MIST ON THE POOL AT DAWN.` → `A BUILDING THAT GLOWS.` → `IT WASN'T ALWAYS GOLD.`

segments.voice: Begin with what it already was: the Harmandir Sahib, also called Darbar Sahib, the court of the Lord. Guru Arjan built it in the middle of the pool at Amritsar and placed the scripture inside. Tradition loves one detail: doors on every side, open to anyone from any direction. Then the hard years, when it was attacked and destroyed more than once, and the misls rebuilt it. Now Ranjit Singh. With a kingdom behind him, he gave the Harmandir its gold. The upper part was covered with copper plates, and the copper was gilded, given a skin of gold. The lower walls were faced with marble, inlaid with stones and flower patterns. Craftsmen worked on it a long time, and slowly the building Sikhs called the Harmandir became the one the world calls the Golden Temple. Here's what matters. He didn't build a temple of his own. He took the Gurus' house, built by Guru Arjan and rebuilt by ordinary Sikhs, and gilded it. Once more, the king's wealth pointed past the king. In the Guru Granth Sahib, a hymn of Guru Arjan says that God himself stood up to finish the work of the saints; tradition links it to the finishing of the pool, and it is still sung when a piece of work is finished. The gold says the same thing in metal: this work is the Guru's, and the best there is belongs here.

Watch the shine come back and notice your hands while they work, with Waheguru on each breath out if you pray.

912.title: A river for a border, 1809
912.hook: a treaty with the British fixes the Sutlej as a boundary
912.howItsDone: Sikh histories remember the treaty of Amritsar, which made the Sutlej the line between Ranjit Singh's kingdom and the British, and santokh, contentment, is named among the virtues in Sikh teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Harmandir, gilded for the Gurus; your line was gold for the guru. Today, a river.

Riders on one bank, the young Maharaja's. On the other, the chiefs who live to the south, nervous, looking over their shoulders. Between them, a wide brown river carrying snowmelt down from the mountains: the Sutlej. And behind them, a new power moving up from the east, the British East India Company, with its own army and its own plans. Two growing powers, one river between them. Somebody has to decide where one ends and the other begins.
screen: `THE SUTLEJ RUNS BETWEEN.` → `NERVOUS CHIEFS TO THE SOUTH.` → `THE COMPANY MOVING UP.`

segments.voice: First, the pressure. Ranjit Singh had been crossing the Sutlej, drawing the chiefs south of it into his orbit. Some of them, including the Phulkian houses this path met earlier, turned to the British for protection, and the Company sent an envoy, Charles Metcalfe, to the Maharaja's camp. Second, the bargain. The talks were tense, and the histories say they nearly broke more than once. In the end, at Amritsar, the two sides signed a treaty. The Sutlej would be the line. South of it, the British would protect the chiefs. North of it, the Maharaja was free to build his kingdom, and the Company would leave him alone. Third, what it cost and what it gave. It cost him a dream of ruling all the Sikh lands on both banks, a real loss. But it gave him peace on his eastern side, and he turned his energy north and west instead. The histories say he kept his word: as long as he lived, he did not cross that line in force. In Japji, Guru Nanak says the bull that holds the earth in place is dharma, born of compassion, and that contentment is the thread holding it steady. Santokh, contentment, is a Sikh virtue. Not giving up: knowing where your line is, and letting that knowledge hold your world steady. A powerful man, drawing a line he could have pushed.

913.title: A modern army
913.hook: he trains his army with European officers alongside Sikh generals
913.howItsDone: Sikh histories remember Ranjit Singh's army, trained in part by European officers and led by Sikh and Punjabi generals; the Guru Granth Sahib includes the hymns of the Gurus alongside those of saints from many backgrounds, Hindu and Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sutlej, a river line he chose to keep; your line was the river line. Today, a parade ground.

A parade ground outside Lahore, early morning. Rows of foot soldiers in matching jackets march in step to drums, turn on one command, and fire together. Officers shout orders in a mix of languages. Some are Punjabi chiefs whose families rode with the misls. Some have come from very far away, from France and Italy, men who learned soldiering in the wars of Europe. The misls fought as bands of horsemen. This is something new.
screen: `A PARADE GROUND OUTSIDE LAHORE.` → `DRUMS, DRILL AND VOLLEYS.` → `OFFICERS FROM FAR AWAY.`

segments.voice: Ranjit Singh had a problem. The misl way of fighting, fast riders striking and vanishing, had won the Punjab. But across the river he had seen the British, with trained infantry and artillery that fought as one machine. He could ignore that, or learn from it. He learned. He built new regiments of infantry and artillery drilled in the European way, and hired European officers to train them, among them Jean-Baptiste Ventura and Jean-François Allard, who had served in Napoleon's armies. Accounts say he set them conditions: to respect Sikh ways in his lands and, some sources say, not to eat beef or smoke. They taught drill and gunnery, and some led the new regiments on campaign. But the Maharaja kept command in his own hands, and his great campaigns were led by his own generals, Sikh and Punjabi. Learning from outside is not new in Sikh history. The Guru Granth Sahib holds the Gurus' hymns beside those of saints from very different backgrounds: Kabir the weaver, Ravidas the leatherworker, Namdev the tailor, and Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi. In Sikh telling, those words were placed in the scripture for what they say, not for where their writers came from, and Guru Arjan gathered them into the book himself. The parade ground was a long way from the Granth. But the habit underneath was the same: truth and skill can come through anyone.

914.title: Hari Singh Nalwa
914.hook: his great general held the north-west frontier and died at Jamrud
914.tomorrow: The Maharaja at the Akal Takht
914.howItsDone: Sikhs tell stories of Hari Singh Nalwa as a general of great courage, and some connect his story with Kabir's verse about the true hero who never leaves the field.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a modern army: European drill, Sikh command, and a king willing to learn; your line was learn from all. Today, one of the generals who led it.

Rocky hills. A narrow pass climbing west into the mountains: the Khyber. At its mouth stands a fort called Jamrud, and inside it a small garrison is waiting for a fight. Somewhere in the hills an army is coming down. The man responsible for this edge of the kingdom is a general whose name, the stories say, had become a word for nerve. When he falls, the fort still has to hold.
screen: `THE MOUTH OF THE KHYBER.` → `A SMALL GARRISON AT JAMRUD.` → `A NAME THAT MEANT NERVE.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tradition explains Nalwa with a story: on a hunt, a tiger sprang at the young Hari Singh, and he fought it and killed it. Whether every detail is true or not, the name stuck to him like armor. Next, the job. Ranjit Singh's kingdom reached toward the mountains of the north-west, toward Peshawar and the Khyber. That edge was hard to hold: rough country, local powers with their own claims, and a kingdom in Kabul that claimed the same ground. Hari Singh Nalwa was sent to hold it. He governed, built forts and kept the passes. Then Jamrud. Tradition tells it like this. An Afghan army came down to the fort. Hari Singh rode out to relieve it and was mortally wounded in the fighting. As he lay dying, he asked his men to keep his death a secret, so that defenders and enemy alike would think he was still in command until help could arrive. They did, and tradition says the fort held. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Kabir says the true hero is the one who fights for the deen, a word some read as the helpless and some as the faith, and who would be cut to pieces before leaving the field. Some Sikhs hear that line in stories like this one. The story honors not glory or the size of the battle, but a man who stood at the edge so others could live behind it, and who even in dying thought about who would hold the line.

915.title: The Maharaja at the Akal Takht
915.hook: tradition says the Nihang leader Akali Phula Singh summoned Ranjit Singh to the Akal Takht for penance and he came humbly
915.howItsDone: Sikhs regard the Akal Takht in Amritsar as the seat from which the Khalsa can call any Sikh to account, and the story of Ranjit Singh accepting Akali Phula Singh's summons is told as an example that no Sikh stands above it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nalwa, the general who held the frontier even as he died; your line was the frontier held. Today, a summons.

A message arrives at the palace in Lahore. It isn't from a rival king or the British. It comes from the Akal Takht at Amritsar, addressed to the Maharaja himself, and it says, in effect: you have broken Sikh discipline; come and answer for it. The man who sent it has no kingdom. He leads a band of Nihangs, fierce, plain-living Sikh warriors. The man receiving it rules the Punjab. Everyone at court waits to see what he'll do.
screen: `A SUMMONS FROM AMRITSAR.` → `ADDRESSED TO THE MAHARAJA.` → `SENT BY A MAN WITH NO KINGDOM.`

segments.voice: First, the place. The Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One, faces the Harmandir across the walkway at Amritsar. Sikh tradition says Guru Hargobind raised it as the seat where the community's worldly affairs would be decided before God. From there, the Khalsa can call any Sikh to account. Any Sikh. Next, the man. Akali Phula Singh was a Nihang leader known for courage and strictness, and tradition remembers him serving at the Akal Takht. He fought in Ranjit Singh's campaigns. But when, as the story goes, the Maharaja's own conduct broke Sikh discipline, Phula Singh did not look away. He summoned him. Then the moment. Tradition says Ranjit Singh came, not with soldiers, but on foot, with folded hands. He admitted the wrong and accepted the punishment given, by the common telling a flogging, and bared his back. The gathered Sikhs, seeing the ruler of the Punjab with his head bowed, were so moved that they cried out for mercy, and the punishment was set aside for a fine. Notice who's above whom. In the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the king spoke of serving the Khalsa. Here, for one morning, it wasn't just a phrase. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that sweetness and humility are the essence of every virtue. The Maharaja who laughed about his one eye could also bow his head.

916.title: Multan, 1818
916.hook: the city of saints and heat joins the kingdom
916.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the janamsakhi story of Guru Nanak's jasmine flower on the bowl of milk at Multan, and Sikh histories remember the siege of Multan and the courage of its governor, Nawab Muzaffar Khan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Akal Takht, where even the king bowed; your line was even the king bowed. Today, far to the south.

Heat that hits like an open oven door. Dust in the air, the sun white overhead, and rising out of the haze, the domes of shrines, glazed in blue and white tiles. Multan, far down in the south of the Punjab. Some call it a city of saints, for its Sufi shrines, and a city of heat, for reasons you can feel on your skin. It has a fort, and a governor inside it who has no intention of giving it up.
screen: `HEAT LIKE AN OVEN DOOR.` → `BLUE-TILED SHRINES IN THE HAZE.` → `A GOVERNOR IN THE FORT.`

segments.voice: Start long before the kingdom. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Nanak coming to Multan on his travels, and the janamsakhis, the old stories of his life, tell it this way. The holy men of the city, hearing a new teacher had arrived, sent him a bowl of milk filled to the brim. The message was polite and clear: this city is already full of saints; there's no room for one more. Guru Nanak laid a small jasmine flower on the milk. It floated, and not a drop spilled. His answer: I won't take your room; I'll only add a fragrance. Now the siege. Ranjit Singh had tried for Multan before and been turned back. This time his army came to stay, with heavy guns, and the fort was surrounded through the heat. Its governor, Nawab Muzaffar Khan, refused to surrender. Tradition says that when the walls were finally breached, he came out sword in hand with his sons beside him and fought until he fell. Sikh accounts remember his courage with respect. An enemy can be honored. Then Multan, with its shrines, its markets and its long road to the south, became part of the kingdom, which now reached deep into the south of the Punjab. Put the two stories side by side: a flower that doesn't spill the milk, and a governor who wouldn't yield. Multan joins, but the city of saints stays a city of saints.

segments.voice: Let your mind travel to the hottest place you've ever stood, a summer street, a kitchen in July, a beach at noon, and feel the heat, the light pressing on your eyelids, the slowness it brings. Then let a small cool thing arrive, a breeze, a cup of water, a white flower floating on milk, and let your breath slow around it, with Waheguru if you pray.
Multan. The city of saints and heat, where Guru Nanak laid a flower on the milk, and which joined Ranjit Singh's kingdom after a hard siege. Today's word.
Your line: multan joins. A fragrance added, nothing spilled. Day nine hundred sixteen, and counting.

917.title: Kashmir, 1819
917.hook: the valley comes under Sikh rule
917.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the Kashmir campaign in histories of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's reign, where it is told as one of the conquests that took the kingdom into the mountains.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Multan, the hot city of saints, and your line, multan joins. Today we climb out of the plains into the mountains, and close the week.

Snow on the passes. A lake with houseboats. Fields of saffron, and shawls so fine, the old stories say, that one could be drawn through a ring. That's Kashmir, the valley ringed by mountains north of the Punjab. For a long time it had been ruled from far away, by governors sent from Kabul. Then, as Sikh histories tell it, an army came up the mountain roads from Lahore, dragging its guns behind it.
screen: `SNOW, SAFFRON, SHAWLS.` → `A VALLEY RULED FROM FAR AWAY.` → `AN ARMY FROM LAHORE.`

segments.voice: Start with the road. Getting an army into Kashmir meant hauling men and guns over high passes, and Sikh histories remember that an earlier try had failed. So the second was planned with care. The Maharaja sent his general, Misr Diwan Chand, a Hindu officer who had risen in his service, with Sikh commanders beside him. The army crossed the mountains, met the Afghan governor's forces, and won the valley. Then the change at the top. Kashmir had been held for the kings in Kabul; now its governors were named in Lahore. Histories tell of Kashmir's shawls and saffron reaching the Lahore court, and of the Maharaja's love of fine Kashmiri things. Now the honest part. Ruling a valley is harder than winning one. Some governors sent from Lahore are remembered well, some less so, and Kashmiri memory of these years is mixed. That belongs in the story too. And look back at this week: gold laid on the Harmandir, a river fixed as a border, an army trained by teachers from many lands, a general who held the frontier, a Maharaja who bowed to correction at the Akal Takht, Multan in the heat. Day by day, a city became a country. The valley is where the map reached the snow.

segments.voice: Picture mountains on every side of you, close and high, snow on their tops, and down where you sit, sheltered green ground and water moving somewhere nearby. Breathe in the cold, clean air, breathe out slowly, and let the mountains hold the week's noise outside. If you pray, you can say Waheguru quietly on each breath out.
